subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Mixed Strategies and Randomness
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Mixed Strategies and Randomness.

hook.text: A soccer kicker who always goes left is easy to stop. Randomizing left and right makes each individual kick harder.

buildup.text: Mixed strategies involve randomizing choices. Being predictable in competitive games lets opponents exploit your.

discovery.text: Walker and Wooders studied tennis serves and found professionals randomize almost exactly as game theory predicts.

twist.text: Humans are bad randomizers. We avoid repeating the same option and create detectable patterns.

climax.text: In competitive situations, notice if you've a pattern. If your opponent can predict you, your strategy leaks value.

punchline.text: Predictability is a gift to your opponent. Vary your play.

quiz.question: Why are humans bad at mixed strategies?
options: They always choose the mathematically optimal option
They avoid repeating choices and create detectable patterns
They lack understanding of probability theory

details.summary: Mixed strategies involve randomizing between actions with specific probabilities. While Nash equilibrium predicts precise mixing ratios, real players mix imperfectly, showing systematic biases toward patterns and against true randomness.
details.whyItMatters: Mixed strategy equilibria appear in competitive sports, military strategy, and business competition. Understanding how humans deviate from optimal mixing reveals exploitable patterns in any competitive setting.
takeaways: Nash equilibrium predicts specific randomization probabilities
Humans are poor randomizers and exhibit predictable patterns
Professional athletes approximate mixed strategies but show exploitable biases

faq.question: Do sports players actually play mixed strategies?
faq.answer: Approximately. Soccer penalty kickers and tennis servers mix directions at roughly equilibrium rates, but they show serial correlation, switching directions too frequently after a failed attempt rather than randomizing independently each time.

faq.question: Why are humans bad at being random?
faq.answer: Human brains seek patterns and avoid repetition even when true randomness requires occasional repetition. People alternate too much, avoid streaks, and show the gambler's fallacy, creating predictable pseudo-random sequences.
